name: Weighted Lap Pad Quiet Time
materials_needed: Weighted lap pad or heavy blanket
steps: Find a quiet spot away from bright lights and loud sounds
Place the weighted pad on the child's lap or shoulders
Sit together or let the child sit alone for 5-10 minutes
Offer a calm activity (book, soft music) if the child wants one
why_it_helps: Deep pressure input is calming for many children because it activates the proprioceptive and tactile systems in a way that reduces overall arousal — commonly used in OT sensory diets.

name: Bear Hug Deep Pressure Squeeze
steps: Ask the child if they'd like a tight hug (always ask first — consent matters)
Give a firm, sustained squeeze hug for 10-20 seconds
Release slowly, check in on how they feel
Repeat 2-3 times if the child wants more
why_it_helps: Firm, sustained pressure is regulating for many children with sensory sensitivities, similar in effect to a weighted blanket, and strengthens connection through a child-led, consent-based interaction.

name: Slow Swing Time
steps: Settle the child into the swing securely
Push or rock gently and slowly, avoiding sudden speed changes
Keep movement rhythmic and predictable
Narrate calmly if the child finds words soothing ('slow... and... slow...')
why_it_helps: Slow, rhythmic vestibular (movement) input tends to calm the nervous system, while fast or unpredictable movement tends to excite it — useful distinction for regulation-focused play.

name: Animal Walk Obstacle Course
steps: Set up a simple path (crawl under a table, step over cushions, hop to the end)
Demonstrate 'animal walks' — bear crawl, frog jump, crab walk — along the path
Have the child do 2-3 laps, switching animals each time
Cool down with a slow walk at the end
why_it_helps: Heavy, whole-body movement provides alerting proprioceptive input that can help an under-aroused or inattentive child become more organized and ready to focus afterward.

name: Textured Sensory Bin Exploration
materials_needed: Small scoops/cups/toys to bury and find
steps: Fill the bin with the chosen material
Hide a few small toys inside
Let the child dig, scoop, and search with hands or tools
Follow the child's lead on how long and how intensely they engage
why_it_helps: Tactile exploration at the child's own pace builds tolerance for varied textures over time and offers a low-pressure way to engage sensory-seeking behavior constructively.

name: Bubble Popping Chase
steps: Blow a stream of bubbles into open space
Encourage the child to chase and pop them
Pause occasionally and wait for the child to request 'more' (verbally, with a sound, or by reaching)
Celebrate each pop with enthusiasm
why_it_helps: The pause-and-wait structure creates natural opportunities for communication attempts, while the visual/motor chase is highly motivating and low-demand.

name: Cause-and-Effect Toy Play
materials_needed: Pop-up toys, switch-activated toys, or simple musical toys
steps: Show the child the toy's action once (press button, music plays)
Place the child's hand near the trigger and let them try
Repeat, gradually reducing your physical help
Keep sessions short and stop while the child is still interested
why_it_helps: Cause-and-effect toys teach a foundational concept — 'my action changes the world' — which is especially valuable for children with significant developmental delay who are building early engagement and intentionality.

name: Special-Interest Story Time
materials_needed: Books, videos, or toys related to the child's special interest
steps: Choose material tied directly to the child's current special interest
Read, watch, or play together, letting the child lead the pace
Ask open questions about what they notice ('What's your favorite part?')
Follow tangents the child introduces rather than redirecting to 'stay on topic'
why_it_helps: Building on a child's special interest dramatically increases engagement and motivation, and research-informed practice treats special interests as a strength to build from, not something to redirect away from.

name: Clothespin Pinching Game
materials_needed: A cup, box edge, or small container
steps: Show the child how to pinch open a clothespin and clip it to an edge
Let the child clip 5-10 clothespins around a cup or box edge
Make it a game — clip by color, or race against a timer
Reverse the task — unclip them all
why_it_helps: The pinching motion directly strengthens the small hand muscles used in handwriting and buttoning, making it a targeted fine-motor exercise disguised as play.

name: Obstacle Course: Crawl, Climb, Balance
materials_needed: Cushions, a low step or stool, a taped line on the floor
steps: Set up 3-4 stations: crawl under a table, step over cushions, walk along a taped line, climb onto a low stool
Demonstrate the course once
Let the child go through at their own pace, offering a hand for balance stations if needed
Repeat 2-3 times, celebrating effort over speed
why_it_helps: Sequencing different gross-motor challenges in one course builds coordination, balance, and body awareness incrementally, with each child progressing at their own level of support.

name: Playdough Squeeze and Roll
steps: Give the child a ball of playdough to squeeze, pull, and roll
Introduce simple shapes with cutters if the child is interested
Encourage rolling 'snakes' and pinching 'pancakes' flat
Let the child direct what they want to make
why_it_helps: Squeezing and manipulating resistant materials strengthens hand muscles used for handwriting and self-care tasks, while remaining an open-ended, low-pressure activity.

name: Choice Board Snack Time
materials_needed: Pictures of each snack (printed or drawn) or the real items visible
steps: Lay out 2-3 snack choices where the child can see or point to each
Ask 'Which one?' and wait quietly, giving the child time to respond however they can (pointing, picture, word, sound)
Honor whatever communication attempt the child makes by giving that snack
Repeat across the week to build the expectation that communication gets a response
why_it_helps: Offering structured choices creates low-pressure, motivating opportunities to practice requesting — a foundational communication skill — and works for children at very different language levels.

name: Picture Schedule Walk-Through
materials_needed: 3-5 pictures or icons representing steps of a routine (e.g. brush teeth, get dressed, eat breakfast)
steps: Lay out the pictures in order on a strip or board
Point to each picture as that step happens
Let the child move or flip the picture to 'done' once completed
Praise completion of each step, not just the whole routine
why_it_helps: Visual schedules reduce anxiety around transitions and give non-verbal or emerging-verbal children a way to understand and predict 'what happens next' without relying on spoken instructions alone.

name: Turn-Taking Ball Roll
steps: Sit facing the child a short distance apart
Roll the ball to the child and say 'your turn'
Wait for them to roll it back, prompting gently if needed
Add a word cue each turn ('roll!', 'go!') to pair the action with language
why_it_helps: Simple back-and-forth games build the foundational social-communication skill of reciprocal turn-taking, which underlies conversation later on.

name: Mirror Game
steps: Stand facing the child and say 'copy me!'
Make a simple movement or facial expression (wave, smile, clap)
Let the child copy you, then switch — you copy them
Keep it playful and exaggerated to hold attention
why_it_helps: Mirroring builds joint attention and social reciprocity in a fun, pressure-free format, and taking turns leading/following practices flexible social roles.

name: Simple Board Game Turn-Taking
materials_needed: A short, simple board game or card game (e.g. a matching or color game)
steps: Choose a short game with clear, simple rules
Model saying 'your turn' and 'my turn' out loud
Play through 1-2 rounds, prompting turn-taking language as needed
Acknowledge both winning and losing calmly to model good sportsmanship
why_it_helps: Structured games provide clear, predictable rules for practicing turn-taking, waiting, and handling the emotions of winning/losing — skills that are harder to teach in unstructured social settings.

name: Parallel Play With a Shared Toy Bin
materials_needed: A bin of toys with duplicates (two of some items) shared between child and a sibling/parent/peer
steps: Sit near the child, each with access to the shared bin
Play alongside the child with a similar toy, without requiring direct interaction
Occasionally comment on what you're doing ('I'm building a tower')
Let interaction emerge naturally rather than forcing shared play
why_it_helps: For children not yet ready for interactive play, parallel play is a well-established bridge step — it builds comfort being near others engaged in a similar activity before direct social interaction is expected.
